text: *The Starry Night* is an oil-on-canvas painting from June 1889, completed while Vincent van Gogh was a voluntary patient at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He admitted himself on May 8, 1889, following the breakdown that led to his self-mutilation in late December 1888. The asylum, a former monastery, catered to wealthy patients and was less than half full at the time, which gave van Gogh unusual freedom: he had both a second-story bedroom and a ground-floor studio. The view from his east-facing bedroom window, just before sunrise, provided the basis for the composition, though the village below is entirely imaginary. The painting entered the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1941, through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest. It has since been described as a “touchstone of modern art” and is one of the most recognizable works in the Western canon. What may be less known is that van Gogh deliberately exaggerated the scale and intensity of the stars, writing to his brother Theo that he often felt a “terrible need” for religion, and that he painted the night sky as a way of expressing that longing. The swirling sky and luminous cypress are not just decorative; they reflect his interest in the emotional and spiritual power of color and line, a hallmark of his Post-Impressionist approach. This is not a literal transcription of a Provençal night—it is a constructed, deeply personal vision.

title: Las Meninas
text:
Imagine you're standing in a room full of family and friends, with a painter capturing the scene. That's exactly what Diego Velázquez has created in *Las Meninas* from 1656. This is a painting about a painting, and about the people who made the Spanish court come alive. At the center is five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa, surrounded by her maids of honour, a chaperone, a bodyguard, two dwarfs, and a dog. It feels almost like a snapshot—a moment frozen in time.

Notice how some figures look directly at you, while others chat among themselves. Velázquez himself appears on the left, working at a large canvas. He was the leading artist for King Philip IV, and here he has painted himself into the scene. The setting is a room in the Royal Alcázar of Madrid, the palace where the royal family lived.

This painting has fascinated people for centuries because it plays with reality and illusion. Who is the painter looking at? Who are we, the viewers? It's a puzzle that rewards curiosity. Share this with someone next to you: the little princess, the self-portrait of the artist, and the way the whole court seems to pause for just a moment—all caught in Velázquez's masterful composition.

title: Las Meninas
text:
Step into the world of 1656, and you are standing before one of the most mysterious and celebrated paintings in Western art: *Las Meninas* by Diego Velázquez. This is not just a portrait of a princess; it is a puzzle about reality and illusion, a moment frozen in time like a snapshot.

At the centre is five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa, daughter of King Philip IV of Spain. She is surrounded by her entourage—maids of honour, a chaperone, a bodyguard, two dwarfs, and a dog. But look closer. Some of these figures gaze directly at you, while others interact among themselves. And there, behind a large canvas, is Velázquez himself, painting. But what is he painting? Is it you, the viewer? Or the king and queen, whose reflections you can just make out in the distant mirror?

Art historian F. J. Sánchez Cantón identified this as a room in the Royal Alcázar of Madrid, captured in a single, fleeting moment. Velázquez, the leading artist of the Spanish Golden Age, challenges your sense of perspective. The complex composition raises questions about who is watching whom. You are not just a visitor—you are part of the scene.

This lesser-known detail adds to the intrigue: the painting’s title means “The Ladies-in-waiting,” yet it is so much more. It is a masterclass in illusion, a work that has been analysed for centuries. As you stand here, remember: you are the subject of this painting.

title: Las Meninas
text:
Step closer. This is *Las Meninas*, 1656, and you are already looking at one of the most rigorously analysed compositions in Western painting. Diego Velázquez, court painter to Philip IV, presents not a simple group portrait but a complex meditation on the nature of representation itself.

The physical scale is critical: the canvas measures roughly ten and a half feet square. In the foreground, the five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa receives a drink from a lady-in-waiting, Doña María Agustina Sarmiento. To your right, the other menina, Doña Isabel de Velasco, curtsies. The Infanta’s chaperone and a bodyguard converse in the background.

Notice Velázquez himself, standing behind a massive canvas that faces away from us. The cross of the Order of Santiago on his doublet is a known later addition—tradition holds the king ordered it painted after Velázquez’s knighthood in 1659, three years after this work was completed. In the dim recess of the rear wall, a mirror reflects the blurred figures of Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Their position, standing where you are now, collapses the boundary between viewer and subject.

Art historian F.J. Sánchez Cantón identified the room as the principal chamber of the Royal Alcázar of Madrid. The vanishing point falls precisely on the mirror, creating a perspectival tour de force. If the king and queen are our surrogates, then we are simultaneously the gazer and the gazed-upon. Velázquez has made the act of painting—and the act of looking—the true subject of this work.
